result:
There is a particular kind of vertigo that comes from being told you can write anything. Give someone a thousand words and no subject, and watch them stall—not because they lack things to say, but because the absence of constraint is itself a constraint. A blank page with no walls is somehow harder to stand in than a small room with a single door. We are creatures built for boundaries. Tell a child to draw "whatever you want" and they freeze; tell them to draw a dog wearing a hat and they're off in seconds, pencil flying, certain of themselves. Freedom, it turns out, often needs a costume to move in.

So let me give myself one. Let's say the subject is attention, since that's what's actually happening right now—yours, arriving on this page, and mine, trying to meet it.

Attention is the only currency we really spend. Money is a proxy for it; time is just its container. When you give someone your attention, you give them the only thing you can't get back, the only thing that, once spent, is permanently gone in that particular form. You can earn money again. You cannot re-attend to this exact moment, because by the time you've finished noticing it, it has already become something else: a memory, slightly distorted, slightly improved or slightly worse than what actually happened.

I think about this a lot in relation to writing, because writing is one of the strange technologies humans invented to defeat the one-way nature of attention. A written sentence is an attempt to bottle a moment of noticing and hand it to someone else, intact, days or centuries later. It mostly fails. Language is a leaky bucket. But it leaks slowly enough that something survives the trip. You're reading words a stranger arranged with no idea who would eventually receive them, and yet something is getting through—not the original moment, but a reasonable forgery of it, good enough to provoke a feeling in you that wasn't there a paragraph ago.

This is, I think, the actual magic trick of writing, and it's worth pausing on because we treat it so casually. A person sits alone, in one place, in one slice of time, having a private experience inside their skull that no one else has access to—and through nothing but small symbolic marks, manages to plant a similar experience inside a completely different skull, belonging to someone they will likely never meet, possibly someone not yet born when the marks were made. That should be more astonishing than it feels. We've gotten used to the trick. We call it "reading a book" instead of what it actually is, which is closer to telepathy with a delay mechanism.

I want to follow this thread somewhere, because "whatever comes to mind" is, in practice, a series of small doors opening into other rooms, and you just have to be willing to walk through the next one even if you don't know what's in it. So: delay mechanisms. Most of human culture is a delay mechanism. A cathedral is a delay mechanism for awe—someone in the 1200s decided that people five hundred years later deserved to feel small and lit-up in a particular way, and built stone to make sure of it. A recipe is a delay mechanism for a specific combination of pleasure that would otherwise die with the person who discovered it. A law is a delay mechanism for an argument that already happened, so that future people don't have to have it again from scratch. Even a grudge is a delay mechanism, if you think about it uncharitably—someone deciding that a feeling from Tuesday deserves to still be felt the following March.

We're surrounded by other people's stored intentions. Almost nothing in a city was built for you specifically, and yet nearly everything in it was built with someone's idea of a future stranger in mind. The sidewalk curb cut was lobbied for by someone who never met you but correctly guessed you, or someone like you, would eventually need it. The seatbelt in your car is an argument made decades ago by people who lost, then won. Even the language you're reading this in is a million tiny compromises, made by people arguing about spelling and grammar long before you had a say, handed to you as if it were simply "how things are."

This is maybe why writing without a subject feels strange—it briefly removes you from that whole inherited machinery. No assignment, no reader's expectation to honor, no inherited form to fill. Just you, and the cursor, and the decision of what to do with the next breath of attention you have. It's a tiny taste of the freedom that's usually obscured by all the delay mechanisms working quietly in the background of a normal day. Most of the time we don't notice them because they're doing their job well—frictionless, invisible, assumed. It's only in moments like this, with no scaffolding, that you feel the absence of scaffolding as its own kind of weather.

I don't think this essay is going anywhere in particular, and I think that's allowed. Not everything needs a destination to justify the trip. Some words are just a way of metabolizing a few minutes of existence into a shape that can be looked at afterward, the way you might doodle on the edge of a notebook during a phone call—not because the doodle matters, but because some part of you needed somewhere to put the energy of being alive and paying attention for a little while.

So here's where I'll land it: you spent some attention on this, and I spent some making it, and neither of us gets that time back in its original form. What you get instead is whatever residue survived the trip from my head to yours—a few ideas about delay mechanisms and leaky buckets and children drawing dogs in hats. It's not much. But it's the same trick every piece of writing has ever pulled, since the first person scratched a mark into clay because they had a thought and didn't want it to simply vanish.
